lesson.title: Building Blocks of Energy: Enthalpy of Formation
lesson.summary: The standard enthalpy of formation, delta Hf degree, is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states, with every element in its standard state defined to have a formation enthalpy of exactly zero.
lesson.body:
A formation reaction is a very specific kind of reaction: it produces exactly one mole of a single compound from its elements, each element in its standard state. This idea connects directly to what you already know about compounds, since only a compound, made of two or more different elements bonded together, can actually be formed this way. An element reacting with itself does not count as a formation reaction. The standard enthalpy of formation, written delta Hf degree, is defined as the enthalpy change of that specific formation reaction, reported per mole of compound produced.

By definition and convention, the standard enthalpy of formation of any element in its standard state is exactly zero. This is not a claim that elements contain no internal energy. It is a reference point, exactly analogous to defining sea level as zero elevation. Every other enthalpy value in a formation table is measured relative to this zero point. So O2(g), graphite (the standard state of carbon), and H2(g) are all assigned delta Hf degree = 0 kJ/mol. But be careful: this zero applies only to an element's actual standard state form. Ozone, O3(g), is not oxygen's standard state (O2 is), so delta Hf degree of O3(g) is not zero, and diamond is not carbon's standard state (graphite is), so delta Hf degree of diamond is not zero either.

The real power of formation values is that they let you calculate the enthalpy change of essentially any reaction without ever running that reaction in a lab, using the relationship delta H degree(rxn) = the sum of moles times delta Hf degree of every product, minus the sum of moles times delta Hf degree of every reactant. This is a direct application of Hess's law: since enthalpy is a state function, you can imagine tearing every reactant apart into its elements (reversing its formation, which flips the sign of its delta Hf degree) and then reassembling those elements into every product (applying its delta Hf degree directly), and the total enthalpy change comes out the same regardless of that imagined path.

As an example, use these standard formation values: delta Hf degree of CO2(g) is negative 393.5 kJ/mol, delta Hf degree of H2O(l) is negative 285.8 kJ/mol, delta Hf degree of CH4(g) is negative 74.8 kJ/mol, and delta Hf degree of O2(g) is 0 kJ/mol by definition. For the combustion of methane, CH4(g) + 2 O2(g) results in CO2(g) + 2 H2O(l), the products sum is (1)(negative 393.5) + (2)(negative 285.8) = negative 393.5 + negative 571.6 = negative 965.1 kJ. The reactants sum is (1)(negative 74.8) + (2)(0) = negative 74.8 kJ. Subtracting gives delta H degree(rxn) = negative 965.1 minus (negative 74.8) = negative 965.1 + 74.8 = negative 890.3 kJ per mole of methane burned. This single calculation, done entirely on paper using tabulated values, reproduces the same strongly exothermic result you would expect to measure directly in a calorimeter, without ever having to burn methane yourself.
